passage:
March: Hrithik had tried everything he could find on his own: breathing videos, a worry journal, cutting out coffee. He still hadn't taken the metro in four months, and he had just said no to his cousin's wedding in Pune. 'I think I need a proper doctor,' he told Pankaj, and felt oddly lighter for saying it.
April: Pankaj offered to come along. In the clinic waiting room he scrolled on his phone and didn't ask a single question. When Hrithik came out holding a referral to a therapist, Pankaj just said, 'Biryani?'
June: after six sessions, Hrithik rode two metro stops with the therapist's plan folded in his pocket. He texted Pankaj a photo of the station sign. Pankaj replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which was exactly right.

qa.q: What did Hrithik come out of the clinic holding?
qa.a: He came out holding a referral to a therapist.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel oddly lighter after telling Pankaj he needed a doctor?
qa.a: Saying it aloud admitted that self-help alone wasn't enough, which seems to have eased the weight of struggling on his own.

qa.q: What did Pankaj get right as a friend?
qa.a: He came along, stayed patient in the waiting room without questioning, and replied simply to the photo, supporting Hrithik without taking over.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pankaj to hold back his questions?
qa.a: Pankaj may be curious and worried, but not asking lets Hrithik own the process, which probably takes some patience.

grounding: It shows a young man whose anxiety keeps limiting his life seeing a doctor and therapist, with a friend who is patient without taking over.

passage:
Ayesha pushed a cup of tea across the pantry table to Keerthana, who had just cancelled her third client visit in a month.
'At twenty-five,' Ayesha said, 'I stopped taking lifts. Then trains. Then I stopped going anywhere I couldn't leave quickly. I read every self-help book in the library. Some helped for a week.
My sister finally said, "Ayesha, you've tried alone for a year. Let a doctor look at this with you." I was embarrassed. I thought only people in real trouble went.
The doctor listened and sent me to a therapist. It wasn't magic; it was months of small, planned steps. My sister never pushed. She drove me to the first few sessions and waited in the car with her crossword.'
Ayesha tapped the table. 'Asking early would have saved me a year.'

qa.q: What did young Ayesha stop taking first?
Why was young Ayesha embarrassed about seeing a doctor?
qa.a: She thought only people in real trouble went, so asking for help felt like admitting something shameful.

qa.q: What might Ayesha be hoping Keerthana will do next?
qa.a: She hopes Keerthana will ask a doctor or trained therapist early, since the cancelled visits suggest the fear is already limiting her work.

qa.q: What was the sister's part in Ayesha's recovery like?
qa.a: The sister was patient: she suggested a doctor, then drove Ayesha to sessions and waited with a crossword, supporting without pushing.

grounding: It shows, through a senior colleague's memory, how seeing a doctor and therapist helped when self-help was not enough, with a sister supporting patiently.
